title: API 653 Training: Online Tank Inspector Exam Prep
description: API 653 exam prep for storage tank inspectors: self-paced online study, instructor Q&A, worked shell and floor calculations, open-book practice.
h1: API 653 Training and Exam Prep for Aboveground Storage Tank Inspectors
html:
The API 653 examination asks you to think like the inspector who signs off an in-service tank. You read a thickness survey and decide whether a shell course or a corroded patch can still hold product at its fill height, judge a floor against the next interval, review a weld procedure, and know where API 650 governs the parts you may not guess. This page sets out what the exam covers under the current Body of Knowledge, works through the calculations that cost candidates the most marks, and explains how the self-paced API 653 exam-prep course and its instructor Q&A fit around a working tank inspection job.

The American Petroleum Institute (API) sets the eligibility rules, administers the API 653 examination and issues the certification. The course prepares you for that examination and has no part in API's process.

What the API 653 exam tests, and is it open book?

API 653 is a 170-question examination: 140 questions are scored and 30 are unscored pretest items that look exactly like the rest. 110 questions are closed-book and 60 are open-book. The day lasts about 7.5 hours, made up of a short tutorial, 2.75 hours on the closed-book part, a 45-minute lunch break and 3.75 hours on the open-book part. You sit it in person at a designated Prometric test centre, with no papers, notes or books of your own; for the open-book part, PDF copies of the relevant codes are on the computer, limited to the sections the Publications Effectivity Sheet lists.

So the honest answer to "is API 653 open book?" is: partly. The Body of Knowledge describes the closed-book part as a test of the everyday working knowledge an inspector carries, and the open-book part as a test of detailed information the inspector is expected to locate in the documents. It adds three warnings worth taking seriously. Some formulas are provided in the exam, but the rules for setting inspection intervals and the formulas for corrosion rate and remaining life may be asked closed-book. Some tables marked in the Body of Knowledge may be asked without the documents. And a calculation may be set in US customary or SI units, so you need to work in both. All calculations apply to existing tanks, not to new construction.

Who should take API 653, and eligibility in brief

API 653 is the certification for inspectors of in-service aboveground storage tanks at refineries, marketing terminals, chemical plants, pipeline tank farms and bulk liquid storage sites. API developed the programme with tank owners and users to give state and local regulators a uniform national benchmark for tank inspection. The people who sit it are tank inspectors working towards certification, NDT technicians who have spent years scanning floors and gauging shells, corrosion and integrity staff, tank construction and repair supervisors, and engineers who review tank inspection reports and repair plans.

Eligibility combines education with storage-tank experience gained in the last ten years while employed by, or under contract with, an authorized inspection agency, as set out in Annex D of API 653. A bachelor's degree in engineering or technology needs one year of supervising or performing inspection; a two-year degree or certificate needs two years; a high school diploma needs three; no formal education needs five or more. On the longer routes the experience can be in design, construction, repair, operation or inspection of tanks, but at least one year must be spent supervising or performing inspection. Military technical service counts on two routes. The full table and how API verifies experience are on the API 653 certification requirements page.

You can start studying before your experience is complete. The course does not count towards the Annex D requirement and does not shorten it; API decides eligibility when it reviews your application.

The API 653 Body of Knowledge and the publications examined

Every exam window has its own Body of Knowledge and Publications Effectivity Sheet. The effectivity sheet API issued for the 2027 windows lists the editions below. Study from the sheet for the window you book, because an addendum or a new edition moves clause numbers and changes values.

The Body of Knowledge is just as useful for what it leaves out. Candidates are not expected to calculate shell thickness for wind, earthquake or small internal pressure, nozzle loads, flanges, venting, ladders and structures, or grillage-supported bottoms, and the variable design point method is not examined. Brazing is out as well. An evening spent on any of those is an evening taken from the shell and bottom questions that carry the marks. For a code-by-code reading of recent changes, see API 653 Body of Knowledge changes explained.

API 653 calculations, with worked examples

The calculations decide most API 653 results. The examples below use one hypothetical tank so you can see how the answers connect: 120 ft nominal diameter, maximum liquid level 40 ft, five courses of 8 ft, product specific gravity 0.9, plate of unknown specification, and records showing an original joint efficiency of 1.0. The figures are practice values; a real evaluation uses the tank's own data and the editions on your effectivity sheet.

Allowable stress S for an existing shell

API 653 takes the allowable product stress from the plate's specified minimum yield strength Y and tensile strength T. For the bottom and second courses, S is the smaller of 0.80Y and 0.429T; for every course above them, the smaller of 0.88Y and 0.472T. When the material is unknown you use Y = 30,000 psi and T = 55,000 psi, which gives 0.429 × 55,000 = 23,595 psi, rounded to 23,600 psi, for the lower two courses and 0.472 × 55,000 = 25,960 psi, rounded to 26,000 psi, above them. Using the upper-course value on the second course is one of the commonest slips on the paper.

Minimum thickness of a whole shell course

For an entire course, API 653 4.3.3.1 gives tmin = 2.6 (H − 1) D G / (S E). H is the height in feet from the bottom of the course to the maximum liquid level, D the nominal diameter in feet and G the highest specific gravity of the contents. The "minus one" is the same idea as the API 650 one-foot method: thickness is set at a point one foot above the bottom of the course. For the first course of the example tank, tmin = 2.6 × (40 − 1) × 120 × 0.9 / (23,600 × 1.0) = 10,951.2 / 23,600 = 0.464 in.

The top course shows the floor in the rule: API 653 never lets tmin fall below 0.1 in. for any course, however small the calculated value.

Corrosion rate and remaining life

The Body of Knowledge gives the corrosion rate as (t previous − t actual) divided by the years between readings, and remaining life as (t actual − t minimum) divided by the corrosion rate; both may be asked closed-book. Suppose the lowest reading on the first course was 0.531 in. six years ago and is 0.507 in. today.

  • Corrosion rate = (0.531 − 0.507) / 6 = 0.004 in. per year.
  • Remaining life = (0.507 − 0.464) / 0.004 = 10.75 years.

Questions like this often hide the trap in the units (readings in millimetres, diameter in metres) or quote the nominal plate thickness where they want the last measured value. Read which thickness the question names before you subtract anything. For when a long-term or short-term rate governs, see long-term and short-term corrosion rates.

A locally thinned area: t1, t2 and the critical length L

For a corroded area, tmin is worked at the lowest point of the area with tmin = 2.6 H D G / (S E), with no minus one. E may be taken as 1.0 where the area is away from any weld by at least the greater of 1 in. or twice the plate thickness. Take a corroded patch in the first course whose lowest point sits 2 ft above the bottom of the course, so H = 38 ft.

  1. tmin = 2.6 × 38 × 120 × 0.9 / (23,600 × 1.0) = 10,670.4 / 23,600 = 0.452 in.
  2. The least thickness in the area excluding pits, t2, is 0.400 in. It must be at least 60% of tmin, which is 0.271 in., so t2 passes.
  3. The critical length L = 3.7 √(D × t2) = 3.7 × √(120 × 0.400) = 3.7 × 6.93 = 25.6 in., inside the 40 in. limit.
  4. Five equally spaced readings over L along the most affected plane are 0.470, 0.455, 0.448, 0.461 and 0.466 in. Their average t1 is 0.460 in., above the 0.452 in. tmin.

The area passes today. Now add the corrosion allowance needed until the next inspection, which API 653 adds to both tmin and the 60% check. At 0.003 in. per year over a five-year run that allowance is 0.015 in., so t1 must reach 0.467 in. and t2 must reach 0.286 in. t1 now fails. The inspector's choices are a shorter run, a lower fill height or a repair. Examiners like this two-stage structure because many candidates stop after the fourth step.

Widely scattered pits

Scattered pits may be ignored if no pit leaves less than half the minimum acceptable shell thickness, excluding corrosion allowance, and the sum of their dimensions along any vertical line is no more than 2 in. in an 8 in. length. On the first course of the example, a pit that leaves less than 0.232 in. of metal has to be evaluated rather than ignored.

Maximum fill height for a thin course

Rearranging the whole-course formula gives the highest liquid level a course will support: H = S E t / (2.6 D G) + 1. If the first course had measured 0.440 in., below its 0.464 in. tmin, then H = 23,600 × 1.0 × 0.440 / (2.6 × 120 × 0.9) + 1 = 10,384 / 280.8 + 1 = 37.98 ft. Rounded down, that course alone would limit the fill to about 37.9 ft until it is repaired. For a locally thinned area the rearrangement drops the added foot. The Body of Knowledge says you are not expected to derive the fill-height formulas and that they are provided in the exam; what it tests is whether you pick the right version.

Hydrostatic test height of a corroded shell

API 653 limits the hydrostatic test height of a corroded shell with a formula of the same shape, using the hydrostatic test stress St in place of S and no specific gravity term, because the test medium is water. When the allowed test height is below the operating height, the owner-operator has to decide whether operating to that height is acceptable. Hydrostatic and leak testing after repairs, alterations and reconstruction are also examined, so learn when a test is required as well as how high it may go.

Bottom plates: minimum remaining thickness and the operating period

API 653 4.4.5.1 projects the floor forward to the next internal inspection. The minimum remaining thickness MRT is the lower of the remaining thickness left by soil-side corrosion (RTbc) and by product-side pitting (RTip), both taken after repairs, minus the operating period Or multiplied by the sum of the unrepaired top-side corrosion rate (StPr) and the soil-side rate (UPr). Take a floor where, after scanning, prove-up and repair, RTbc = 0.17 in., RTip = 0.19 in., StPr = 0.002 in. per year and UPr = 0.006 in. per year.

  • For a ten-year run, MRT = 0.17 − 10 × (0.002 + 0.006) = 0.09 in.
  • The bottom minimum tables (API 653 Tables 4.4a and 4.4b) require 0.10 in. at the next inspection for a bottom with no means of detecting and containing a leak, so ten years fails.
  • Where the design detects and contains a bottom leak, the minimum is 0.05 in. and ten years passes.
  • Against 0.10 in., the longest run is O = (0.17 − 0.10) / 0.008 = 8.75 years, before the interval rules in Section 6 are applied.

The exam provides the formulas for the operating period; your job is to feed them the right inputs, and the coated-floor case, where the top-side rate can be taken as zero under the conditions the standard sets, changes the answer more than most candidates expect. More on floor evaluation in tank floor pitting and minimum remaining thickness and release prevention barriers.

The critical zone

The critical zone is the band of bottom or annular plate within 3 in. of the inside edge of the shell, measured radially inward. Unless a stress analysis is done, the plate there must keep the smaller of half the original bottom plate thickness, excluding the original corrosion allowance, or 50% of tmin of the lower shell course, and never less than 0.1 in. For 0.25 in. bottom plates under the example first course, that is the smaller of 0.125 in. and 0.232 in., so 0.125 in.

Reconstructed shells and the API 650 one-foot method

When a tank is dismantled and rebuilt, the shell is designed again to API 650 with the allowable stresses API 653 sets for reconstruction in 8.4. In US units the design thickness is td = 2.6 D (H − 1) G / Sd + CA and the hydrostatic test thickness is tt = 2.6 D (H − 1) / St, and the larger governs. With illustrative stresses of Sd = 20,000 psi and St = 22,500 psi (read the real values for the plate from API 650 Tables 5.2a and 5.2b), a corrosion allowance of 0.0625 in. and the example first course: td = 10,951.2 / 20,000 + 0.0625 = 0.610 in., and tt = 12,168 / 22,500 = 0.541 in., so the design thickness of 0.610 in. governs.

Hot taps, replacement plates and lap-welded patches

The Body of Knowledge also lists the hot tap requirements in 9.15, including the minimum spacing between an existing nozzle and a new hot tap; the minimum dimensions of replacement shell plates from Figure 9.1; and, for lap-welded patch plates under 9.3, the minimum thickness, the minimum weld size and the allowable patch size. These are mostly look-ups in a figure or a clause, which makes them good open-book marks once you know where they live.

Settlement

Annex B is examined through the tasks the Body of Knowledge names: maximum allowed edge settlement, bottom settlement near the shell, localized bottom settlement remote from the shell, and the number of settlement survey points required under 12.5.2 and Figures B.1 and B.2. Most settlement errors come from reading the figures: which dimension is the deflection, what length or radius it is measured over, and which limit applies to the case in the question. A worked walk-through is in what API 653 Annex B decides about settlement.

Where API 650 catches API 653 candidates

API 650 is a construction standard, but the 653 exam relies on it wherever an existing tank is repaired, altered, reconstructed or re-rated. The Body of Knowledge sends you to it for:

  • Impact testing: the design metal temperature, the Material Group number from API 650 Tables 4.4a and 4.4b, whether testing is required from Figures 4.1a and 4.1b, and whether the impact values are acceptable from Tables 4.5a and 4.5b.
  • Weld sizes for shell and roof openings, from the API 650 nozzle and manhole figures and tables, read alongside API 653 Figures 9.1, 9.2, 9.4 and 9.5.
  • Joint efficiency: the joint type and the type and extent of radiography, from API 653 Section 4 and Section 12 and API 650 8.1 and Figure 8.1, then E from the API 653 joint efficiency tables.
  • General welding rules in API 650 Section 9 and API 653 Section 11, including joint restrictions and reinforcement limits.

Many API 650 annexes are excluded from the exam, among them D, E, F, J, K, L, P, T, V, W, X and Y, and others are examined only in their opening clauses. Leave the excluded annexes until a job needs them. For how the two standards divide the work, see API 650 vs API 653.

Welding and NDE questions: ASME Section IX and Section V

The Body of Knowledge includes a welding procedure review. You are given a WPS with its PQR, and sometimes a welder performance qualification, and asked whether the variables are addressed and whether the mechanical tests and their results are acceptable. It keeps the review narrow: SMAW or GMAW only, one process and one filler metal per record, P-No. 1 base metals, and no dissimilar metals, inserts, overlays, Charpy requirements, supplementary essential variables or heat treatment. Working a dozen such reviews teaches more than reading Section IX from cover to cover.

ASME Section V is examined in Article 1 (general requirements), Article 2 (radiography: location markers, IQIs, density and backscatter), Article 6 (liquid penetrant), Article 7 (magnetic particle, yoke and prod techniques only, excluding T-765 and T-766) and Article 23, limited to SE-797, the practice for manual ultrasonic thickness measurement. API 650 Section 8 and API 653 Section 12 say when each examination is required on a tank. Candidates from NDT usually find these the easiest marks on the paper; candidates from operations or engineering should start them early. For hands-on method training alongside exam prep, see ultrasonic testing training and magnetic particle testing training.

An API 653 study plan, phase by phase

Because the course is self-paced, the plan is organised by phases rather than weeks. Move to the next phase when you can pass the check without your notes.

  1. Set up. Download the Body of Knowledge and Publications Effectivity Sheet for your window, get the listed editions, and read API 653 through once without stopping. Check: you can say which document answers which kind of question.
  2. Closed-book core. The API 653 sections on suitability for service, brittle fracture, inspection, repair and alteration, reconstruction, examination and testing, and records, with Annex B, API RP 575 and the ten RP 571 mechanisms. Check: you can explain the interval rules, change of service and the brittle fracture assessment without the text.
  3. Calculations. Every family above, in both unit systems, until you get the answer and can name the clause. Check: a mixed calculation set with no unit errors.
  4. API 650 and welding. Impact testing, opening welds, joint efficiency and the WPS and PQR review. Check: a clean procedure review at the first attempt.
  5. Supporting practices. The two RP 576 paragraphs, RP 577, RP 651, RP 652 and the Section V articles. Check: definitions and limits you can recall cold.
  6. Exam simulation. Timed closed-book and open-book papers in the real proportions, reviewed question by question. Check: you finish both parts with time in hand and know why each wrong answer was wrong.

Open-book technique for API 653

The open-book part gives you 60 questions in 3.75 hours, about three and three-quarter minutes each. The closed-book part allows 2.75 hours for 110 questions, roughly a minute and a half each, so the two halves need different habits.

  • Learn the map, not the pages. Shell evaluation sits in Section 4, the bottom rules and the remaining-thickness formula in 4.4, settlement in Annex B, hot taps in 9.15 and the reconstruction tolerances in the Section 10 tables.
  • Search the PDF for the code's own words. "Locally thinned" finds the corroded-area rules; "thin spot" finds nothing.
  • Write down the given values before you open a document. Most open-book errors are a correct formula fed the wrong H, E or G.
  • Answer every closed-book question on the first pass, flag the slow ones and come back. A blank scores nothing.
  • Keep both unit systems in view. The Body of Knowledge notes that some tables, such as API 653 Tables 4.1a and 4.1b, are each in a single unit system, so be ready to convert.

How instructor Q&A helps on tank questions

The questions API 653 candidates send while studying tend to fall into a few groups: which H to use for a thinned area that crosses into the course above, whether E is 1.0 or the original joint efficiency for a patch near a weld, how the top-side rate is handled on a partly coated floor, and why a WPS that looks complete fails because its PQR does not support one of the ranges. Each answer takes you to the clause and table that settle the point, so the next question of that kind is quicker. You can send a question at any stage of your self-paced study, including while you are working through practice papers.

After the API 653 exam: certification and recertification

API scores the examination and issues the certificate; the course has no part in either. API 653 certification runs for three years and is ANSI-accredited under ISO 17024. To recertify you apply through the ICP Portal from 90 days before expiry, with a 90-day grace period that carries late fees. You must show that at least 20% of your time over the last three years went on performing or supervising tank inspection, or sit the full exam again, and you need 24 hours of continuing professional development per three-year cycle across at least two categories. Every six years there is also an open-book web quiz of 25 questions on code changes, with four hours allowed, up to three pauses and one retake after a failure. Owners and contractors can confirm a certificate in API's directory; see how to verify an API inspector certificate.

Sponsoring API 653 candidates as an employer

Tank owners, terminal operators and inspection contractors often sponsor more than one candidate, because a single certified inspector rarely covers a whole tank farm's out-of-service programme. Each sponsored candidate applies to API on their own, sits the exam on their own appointment and works through the course around rotations and turnarounds. Fees are quoted on request for one candidate or a group. If your tanks are moving to risk-based intervals, Atlantis also carries out remote storage tank RBI studies for owner-operators; see storage tank RBI. The ASNT NDT training the same crews need for thickness gauging and MT and PT work is under NDT training courses.

faq.q: Is the API 653 exam open book?
faq.a: Partly. Of the 170 questions, 110 are closed-book and 60 are open-book. In the open-book part, PDFs of the code sections on the Publications Effectivity Sheet are on the test computer; you cannot bring your own books or notes. The Body of Knowledge also warns that the interval rules and the corrosion-rate and remaining-life formulas may be asked closed-book, so commit them to memory.

faq.q: Do I need to know API 650 for the API 653 exam?
faq.a: Yes, in the areas the Body of Knowledge names: impact testing, weld sizes for shell and roof openings, joint efficiency and radiography extent, welding rules, and the allowable stresses and one-foot formulas used for reconstructed shells. Many API 650 annexes are excluded. Treat API 650 as the reference behind repair, alteration and reconstruction questions rather than as a design course.

faq.q: Which API 653 calculations come up most?
faq.a: Corrosion rate and remaining life; shell minimum thickness for whole courses and for locally thinned areas, with t1, t2 and the critical length L; pitting limits; maximum fill height; bottom minimum remaining thickness and operating period; settlement from Annex B; hot tap spacing; lap-welded patch plates; and impact testing from API 650. The API 653 shell minimum thickness guide covers the shell rules in more depth.

faq.q: Are the formulas given to you in the API 653 exam?
faq.a: Some are. The Body of Knowledge says the fill-height formulas and the formulas for the bottom operating period are provided, but the rules for setting inspection intervals and the formulas for corrosion rate and remaining life may be asked closed-book. Learn the shell tmin formulas and the rate and life formulas well enough to use them without looking anything up.

faq.q: Can I start the API 653 course before I have the required experience?
faq.a: Yes. Many candidates study while they build their experience. The course does not count towards the Annex D requirement or reduce it, and API decides your eligibility when you apply. Check your education and experience route on the API 653 certification requirements page before you choose an exam window.

faq.q: Does the course include API 653 practice questions?
faq.a: Yes. You work through original practice questions with explanations, calculation drills and timed papers that follow the real split of 110 closed-book and 60 open-book questions. They are written for practice and are not questions from the API examination. Reviewing why each wrong option is wrong is where most of the learning happens.

faq.q: Is the variable design point method on the API 653 exam?
faq.a: No. The Body of Knowledge lists it among the calculations candidates are not expected to perform, together with wind, earthquake and small internal pressure thickness, nozzle loads, flanges, venting, ladders and structures, and grillage-supported bottoms. Time spent on the one-foot formulas, corroded areas and bottom evaluation earns far more marks.

faq.q: Can an employer enrol a group of tank inspectors?
faq.a: Yes. Employers can sponsor several candidates, each studying at their own pace with access to the instructor. Every candidate still applies to API individually and has to meet the eligibility rules in their own right. Tell us how many people you are sponsoring and the window they are aiming at, and we will send the course details and a quote.

faq.q: Is API 579 on the API 653 exam?
faq.a: No. API 579-1/ASME FFS-1 is not one of the publications on the 2027 effectivity sheet. The exam is set on API 653, API 650, RP 571, RP 575, RP 576, RP 577, RP 651, RP 652 and ASME Sections V and IX, within the limits the Body of Knowledge sets for each.
